note: This file now judges the TRADING page. The pro page's iteration-8 judgment is kept verbatim in .design/judgment-pro-page.json; the gate holds one judgment per source tree and both pages share ui/, so the two cannot both live here.

firstFive.what: A terminal trading screen for one perpetual futures account. A live candle chart fills the left with seven overlay toggles above it, and the right stacks account risk, the market's own numbers, a mandate console reading 'Nothing armed', and a running log of what the agent did.
firstFive.who: Someone who trades this account with size they borrowed, and who has an AI agent connected to it. Not a first-time buyer: nothing here explains what a liquidation is.
firstFive.feeling: Instrument panel. Nothing is selling anything. It reads as a machine that will tell you the truth rather than an app that wants you to trade.
firstFive.sibling: Yes, unmistakably the pro page's sibling. Same green on the same near-black, same box-drawing frames with the title notched into the top line, same monospace grid, same status bar shape with the kill switch on the right.
firstFive.wrong: Three of the four right-hand panels are saying a version of 'nothing here'. That is honest, and it is also the whole picture I have of this surface, which is the real problem below.

asked.professional interface, judged against r: Met on content. Liquidation distance is in percent, dollars and ATR at once; profit splits into price, funding and fees; net and gross exposure carry a plain sentence about a five percent move; mark and oracle are separated with the basis in points. Not met yet on one thing the survey ranked highly: there is no size-aware slippage figure, and the spec names it as the next thing to build rather than pretending otherwise.
asked.same design as the pro page: Met. Every colour is a token from style.css, no new hue, no radius, no shadow, no transition. The one extension is red reaching the liquidation surface, which is written into the brief with its reasoning.
asked.manipulable by the agent: Met and proven live. trade_focus moved both this page and the chart to ETH, trade_highlight lit a row, trade_note pinned a line, and a bad overlay name was refused with the list of real ones.
asked.components must not collide: Met now, and it took two real failures to get there. Both are recorded under findings.

goal: A person who has left a bot running can look at this and answer three questions without doing arithmetic: how far am I from being liquidated, how much of what I approved has been spent, and is the screen still telling me the truth.

seen: ARMED with an open position, the mandate console showing its program in English, its four bounds and the arm receipt
working stop orders nested as child rows under the position they protect
a mandate halted by its own notional cap, with the reason in the row
unified account where health is not computable, rendering as a dash over a hatched track
a cross position where the venue returns no liquidation price, so the reverse bar is neutralised rather than fully red
FLATTEN, DISARM and CANCEL ALL driven against live money from the page's own controls
notSeen: a degraded or offline venue banner
a liquidation fill and its ring
a mandate wall drawn INSIDE the visible price range: on every real mandate so far it has sat far below the window and rendered as an edge tag

driven: opened at 1440x900, 768x1024 and 390x844 in a real browser
measured every panel's box against its neighbour at 390: no overlaps
measured scrollWidth against clientWidth at all three: no horizontal scroll anywhere
scrolled to the fills and log boundary at 390 and looked at it, twice, before and after the fix
checked every capped panel for content painting outside its box: none

findings.what: Fill rows painted straight through the log underneath them at 390.
findings.why: An earlier block in trade.css releases every stacked panel to overflow: visible. I later put a height cap back on fills without putting the clip back, and a box 338 pixels tall then painted 550 pixels of rows over the panel below. A height limit with visible overflow is not a compromise, it is the broken case.
findings.note: This is the collision the locked DOM contract was meant to prevent and it was mine, introduced after the contract had done its job.

findings.what: The book table declared seven column headers while the renderer emitted nine cells per row; fills declared seven against eight.
findings.why: My spec's DOM contract and my own ux/flow.md disagreed about the column set, so two agents built to two different truths. Headers now match what is emitted, including NOTIONAL, which was missing from both tables and is a number a trader reads first.

findings.what: An unknown health reading drew as an empty bar.
findings.why: An empty track beside 'health --' says health is at zero, which claims the account is at its liquidation when the truth is that the venue has not published what the figure needs. On a unified account that is the normal case, not an edge one. The track is hatched now, so no signal cannot be misread as a bar that emptied.

findings.what: The command line was bound to an id the markup does not carry, so typing into it did nothing.
findings.why: Same document disagreement as the column set. There is one input now, shared: trade verbs bind in the capture phase and consume what they recognise, and anything else falls through to the chart's own parser.

findings.what: Four hundred pixels of empty right column in the default state.
findings.why: The mandate console held grow while showing one line, which is what this screen shows most of the time. grow moved to the log, and a MARKET panel now fills the space with oracle, basis, open interest, volume and real volatility, all of which were already in the payload and displayed nowhere.

findings.what: The chart's source label truncates to 'hype...' at 1440.
findings.why: It gives up its width first by design so the controls stay on the line, and it is a secondary status. Left alone deliberately.

findings.what: A mandate capped at $60 built a $238 position with 8 orders in one second, on live money.
findings.why: Two causes. setInterval does not wait for an async callback, so eight 250ms ticks ran concurrently through a network call, each reading the order rate and the position before any other had incremented either. And the book handler zeroed in-flight size on every book, so a book that had not caught up with a fill handed the headroom straight back. The loop is serialised, counters increment before the await, and in-flight size is retired by observed position growth with a timeout backstop.
findings.note: Found only by arming a real mandate and looking at the panel. 630 passing tests did not catch it, because every one of them called the checker sequentially.

findings.what: Trigger orders were not counted as orders, and the panel's order meter counted fills rather than orders placed.
findings.why: A rule setting a stop every tick put 104 trigger orders on the venue while the meter read '0 of 4 orders this minute'. set_stop and set_target now count in the envelope and in the runner, and the meter adds working orders to fills. Cancel deliberately still does not count: the venue allows a larger cancel budget on purpose so an account can always cancel its way out.

findings.what: The liquidation bar rendered fully red when the liquidation price is unknown.
findings.why: It is a reverse meter: red track, green fill covering it. A zero-width fill therefore says you are AT your liquidation. The venue returns a null liquidation price on a cross position routinely, so this was the normal state and not a rare one. Neutralised and hatched.

findings.what: The mandate head printed as one unreadable word: BTCARMEDExpires in 3h 11mMANDATE STOP-OUT at --
findings.why: A block of adjacent inline spans with no gap. It is a wrapping flex row with a divider now. Not a styling nit: the state and the expiry became one word on the panel that exists to say what a bot may do.

findings.what: Off-range chart labels all printed at the same edge position and overlapped.
findings.why: An off-pane line drew its own label at a fixed y instead of joining the stacking pass, so a stop below the window and a mandate wall below that came out as '1 STOP $29.20 P 1,860.00 1,133.3'. Off-range is the NORMAL case for a mandate wall, not an edge one. It returns its label to the stacker now.

findings.what: After FLATTEN, the page still listed two mandates as armed.
findings.why: The child stops a mandate on its own during a flatten or a halt, and the host's map did not follow. Misreporting the safety state is the one thing this repo has already decided is worse than the safety being off.

findings.what: The spec claimed the human's wall is ALWAYS nearer than the venue's. It is not.
findings.why: Observed live: stop-out at $1,133 against a projected liquidation at $1,422. The two are computed against different quantities, so a generous loss allowance on a small position puts the stop-out a long way down. The claim is corrected in the spec and the brief; the page draws both and asserts no ordering.
findings.note: This was wrong in my own design document and only real numbers exposed it.

findings.what: The chart's source label truncates to 'hype...' at 1440.
findings.why: It gives up width first by design so the controls stay on the line. Left alone deliberately.

findings.what: The app was found alive but not listening on its port once, after repeated restarts.
findings.why: Not reproduced on a clean start and no crash trace was written. Recorded rather than claimed as fixed, because I do not know what it was.

fixedThisIteration: the live envelope breach: serialised tick, counters before the await, in-flight retired by observed growth
trigger orders counted as orders, and the meter counting orders placed rather than fills
the liquidation bar neutralised when the reading is unknown
mandate head spaced into a wrapping row with dividers
off-range chart labels joined to the stacking pass
the host's armed map cleared when the child halts or flattens
the two-walls claim corrected in the spec and the brief
